```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = FALSE,
  comment = "",
  class.output = "spax-output",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  dpi = 100

Does a finer grid give a better accessibility index, and what does it cost? A
raster gives every place explicit geometry and lines all inputs up cell by
cell. Its cost grows with the number of cells times the number of facilities,
while the result can be no better than the demand and travel data behind it.
This guide runs the enhanced two-step floating catchment area (E2SFCA) index
of [Getting started](spax.html), which gives each place the GP supply per
resident within reach, with weights that fall with travel time. It runs the
index at the native resolution of the bundled grids, at two coarser
resolutions and at one finer resolution, and compares results, size and run
time. By the end you can estimate the memory a grid needs and check whether a
coarser grid would change your answer. The inputs are the mainland grids of
[The Cornwall GP example data](cornwall-data.html). The `spax()` interface and
the allocation model are experimental and may change in later versions.

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
```

## The inputs

The setup code shared by every grid guide, explained in [The Cornwall GP
example data](cornwall-data.html), reads the population grid (residents per
cell), the mainland practices with their GP full-time equivalents (FTE), and
one layer of travel minutes per practice.

```{r inputs}
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel_grid)))
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid, pop)
grid_data <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
```

`grid_data` is the native-resolution input. Below, `index_at()` prepares each
resolution the same way.

## What one cell-by-practice array costs

The travel grid holds one value per cell and practice, and the decay weights
hold another array of the same size. The numeric payload of one such array is
cells times practices times 8 bytes.

```{r storage}
cells <- c(grid = ncell(pop), populated = sum(!is.na(values(pop))))

# 8 bytes per value, one value per cell and practice
data.frame(
  cells,
  practices = nrow(gp),
  MiB_per_array = round(cells * nrow(gp) * 8 / 1024^2, 1)
)
```

The rectangular grid has `r round(cells[["grid"]] / cells[["populated"]], 1)`
times as many cells as its populated part, because it also covers sea and
land outside Cornwall. That is small here. The same arithmetic at 100 meters,
or with hundreds of facilities, reaches gigabytes. spax reads the rasters in
blocks of rows when it computes an FCA index, so it needs less memory than
holding these arrays whole. Measure memory and run time on the whole
workflow: `object.size()` of a terra raster reports only a pointer, not the
cell values.

## Change the resolution

Demand counts can be added up exactly when cells are merged. Travel cannot:
the bundled grids do not contain the road network, so a coarse cell's travel
time has to be approximated from its fine cells. Here we use the
resident-weighted mean of the fine-cell minutes. Averaging travel before a
nonlinear decay does not give averaged weights, so this is one explicit
approximation. For a real study, recompute travel at the target resolution if
you can.

A factor of 2 merges each 2 x 2 block of cells into one, 4 merges 4 x 4
blocks, and 0.5 splits each cell into four. The four subcells of a split cell
each get a quarter of its residents and keep its travel times. This adds cells but
no information.

```{r resample}
# Demand and travel grids at `factor` times the native cell width
at_resolution <- function(factor) {
  # Native grid: unchanged
  if (factor == 1) return(list(demand = pop, travel = travel_grid))

  # Finer grid: split residents evenly, copy the parent's travel times
  if (factor < 1) {
    split <- round(1 / factor)
    return(list(
      demand = disagg(pop, split) / split^2,
      travel = disagg(travel_grid, split)
    ))
  }

  # Coarser grid: add up residents, take resident-weighted mean minutes
  demand <- aggregate(pop, factor, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE)
  minutes <- aggregate(travel_grid * pop, factor, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE) /
    demand
  list(demand = demand, travel = minutes)
}

factors <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 4)
grids <- lapply(factors, at_resolution)
```

Now time the E2SFCA at each resolution, with the Gaussian decay of the other
guides: a travel scale σ of 10 minutes, at which a practice 10 minutes away
keeps `r round(100 * calc_decay(10, method = "gaussian", sigma = 10))`% of
its weight. The timings are elapsed seconds on the machine that
built this guide, the median of three runs. Read them as relative costs.

```{r fit}
e2sfca_spec <- spec_e2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10))

# The E2SFCA index on one resolution's grids
index_at <- function(grid) {
  resolution_data <- prep_data(
    grid$demand,
    gp,
    grid$travel,
    id_col = "practice",
    supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
  )
  spax(resolution_data, e2sfca_spec)
}

# Median elapsed seconds of three runs at each resolution
seconds <- sapply(grids, function(grid) {
  median(replicate(3, system.time(index_at(grid))[["elapsed"]]))
})

results <- lapply(grids, index_at)
```

To compare the results, take each surface back to the native grid: every
native cell gets the value of the cell that contains it. Then compare cell by
cell, weighting by native residents.

```{r compare}
# The native surface and residents, one value per native cell
native <- 1000 * values(results[[2]]$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
residents <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)

# One table row per resolution
summary_row <- function(level) {
  # This surface on the native grid
  on_native <- resample(results[[level]]$accessibility, pop, method = "near")
  on_native <- 1000 * values(on_native, mat = FALSE)

  # Residents and cell area on this resolution's own grid
  demand <- values(grids[[level]]$demand, mat = FALSE)
  area <- values(cellSize(grids[[level]]$demand, unit = "km"), mat = FALSE)

  # Index per 1,000 on its own grid, and the change from the native surface
  own <- 1000 * values(results[[level]]$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
  change <- abs(on_native / native - 1)

  data.frame(
    factor = factors[level],
    cell_km2 = round(mean(area[!is.na(demand)]), 2),
    cells = sum(!is.na(demand)),
    seconds = seconds[level],
    mean_per_1000 = round(weighted.mean(own, demand, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    median_change_pct = round(
      100 * median(change[!is.na(residents)], na.rm = TRUE),
      1
    ),
    mean_change_pct = round(
      100 * weighted.mean(change, residents, na.rm = TRUE),
      1
    )
  )
}

comparison <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(factors), summary_row))
comparison
```

```{r compare-values, include = FALSE}
finer <- comparison[comparison$factor == 0.5, ]
native_row <- comparison[comparison$factor == 1, ]
coarsest <- comparison[comparison$factor == 4, ]
finer_cells <- round(finer$cells / native_row$cells, 1)
finer_time <- round(finer$seconds / native_row$seconds, 1)
coarse_change <- range(comparison$mean_change_pct[comparison$factor > 1])

# Total residents at each resolution (the prose says they are the same)
resident_totals <- sapply(grids, function(grid) {
  global(grid$demand, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
})
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(resident_totals, rep(resident_totals[2], length(grids)))))
total_residents <- format(round(resident_totals[2]), big.mark = ",")
coarse_km2 <- sprintf("%.1f", range(comparison$cell_km2[comparison$factor > 1]))
coarse_speed <- round(native_row$seconds / coarsest$seconds, 1)

# Native cell size: arc-seconds, and kilometers at the middle of the grid
arc_seconds <- round(res(pop)[1] * 3600)
middle <- cbind(mean(ext(pop)[1:2]), mean(ext(pop)[3:4]))
cell_km <- function(step) {
  distance(middle, middle + step, lonlat = TRUE)[1, 1] / 1000
}
north_south_km <- round(cell_km(cbind(0, res(pop)[2])), 2)
east_west_km <- round(cell_km(cbind(res(pop)[1], 0)), 2)
```

`cells` counts the populated cells, and `cell_km2` is their mean area in
square kilometers. The native cells are `r arc_seconds` arc-seconds, often
called 1 km: about `r north_south_km` km north to south but only about
`r east_west_km` km east to west at this latitude. The two change columns give
the median and the resident-weighted mean of the absolute percentage change
from the native surface, over native cells.

Some things stay fixed. Every resolution keeps the same `r total_residents`
residents, and the resident-weighted mean index (`mean_per_1000`) stays at
total GP FTE per 1,000 residents, because both FCA steps use the same
weights. That identity says nothing about local accuracy.

What changes:

- **Finer cells (factor 0.5)** give `r finer_cells` times as many populated
  cells and take `r finer_time` times as long, yet reproduce the native
  surface exactly (a change of `r finer$mean_change_pct`%): no
  information was added.
- **Coarser cells** are cheaper: the 4 x 4 grid runs `r coarse_speed` times
  as fast as the native one, though on a grid this small every run takes a
  fraction of a second. The local pattern changes by `r coarse_change[1]`% to
  `r coarse_change[2]`% for the average resident. A 10-minute decay is wide
  compared with cells of `r coarse_km2[1]` to `r coarse_km2[2]` square
  kilometers, which likely keeps the change small. Repeat the comparison for
  a shorter travel scale or a binary catchment.

The maps put the native surface and the 4 x 4 surface on one color scale.

```{r maps, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Two raster maps of mainland Cornwall on one color scale in GP FTE per 1,000 residents: the native grid on the left and the grid aggregated 4 x 4 on the right; the coarse map keeps the broad pattern, highest in the west between Redruth, Truro and Falmouth, but in larger blocks that blur local detail such as the low values on Bodmin Moor."}
# The native surface and the 4 x 4 surface, both on the native grid
pair <- c(
  1000 * results[[2]]$accessibility,
  resample(1000 * results[[4]]$accessibility, pop, method = "near")
)
names(pair) <- c("Native grid", "Aggregated 4 x 4")

plot(
  pair,
  axes = FALSE,
  col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  range = range(values(pair), na.rm = TRUE),
  mar = c(1, 1, 2, 6),
  plg = list(title = "GP FTE\nper 1,000")
)
```

The coarse surface keeps the broad pattern but blurs the local detail,
including the low values on Bodmin Moor, the upland north-east of the map's
center. Its blocks also cover cells that the native grid leaves empty at the
coast.

## The allocation model

The allocation model of [Where do residents
register?](allocation-workflow.html) estimates the share of each place's
residents who register with each practice. On the small areas, its travel
matrix of areas by practices is small. On raster data every populated cell
becomes an origin, a place residents start from, so the matrix is the
cell-by-practice array above. In the large example of `?prep_data`, a fit to
practice totals from one start peaks at about 8 times that matrix, and the
help page gives its run time too. Read only the tables you need:
`as.data.frame(result, type = "facilities")` (one row per practice) or
`type = "origins"` (one row per origin) is far smaller than `type = "flows"`,
which has a row for every origin and practice with a positive flow. The
bootstrap of [How sure are the
estimates?](facility-bootstrap.html) refits the model for every draw, so its
run time grows with the number of draws.
